lead: A linear map can look abstract, but once you choose a basis it becomes a matrix. Coordinates turn each vector into a column, and the matrix stores where each basis vector goes. This lets a computer multiply matrices instead of calling the map directly. The same map has different matrices in different bases, linked by conjugation. Engineers use this to pick a basis where calculations are simple, such as axes aligned with a robot arm. Some syllabi call this the matrix representation of a linear transformation.
prereq: You need: chapters 3.1, 3.2, 3.3; Unit 1 matrix multiplication; and Unit 2 basis and coordinates.

sections.h3: Coordinates: a vector becomes a column

blocks.text: Fix an ordered basis B = (b<sub>1</sub>, ..., b<sub>n</sub>) of a vector space V. Ordered means b<sub>1</sub> is first, b<sub>2</sub> is second, and so on. Every v in V is a unique combination v = c<sub>1</sub>b<sub>1</sub> + ... + c<sub>n</sub>b<sub>n</sub>. The coordinate vector is [v]<sub>B</sub> = (c<sub>1</sub>, ..., c<sub>n</sub>)<sup>T</sup>. The numbers c<sub>i</sub> are coordinates, not the vector itself. Changing the order of the basis changes the coordinate column.

Example in R² with B = ((1,1), (1,2)). The vector (3,−2) equals 8(1,1) − 5(1,2) = (8−5, 8−10) = (3,−2). So [(3,−2)]<sub>B</sub> = (8,−5)<sup>T</sup>. The ordinary column (3,−2)<sup>T</sup> is the coordinate vector in the standard basis E = (e<sub>1</sub>, e<sub>2</sub>).

Let P be the change-of-basis matrix from B to the standard basis. Its columns are the basis vectors written in standard coordinates. Here P = [[1,1], [1,2]]. Then [v]<sub>E</sub> = P[v]<sub>B</sub>, and [v]<sub>B</sub> = P<sup>−1</sup>[v]<sub>E</sub>. The matrix P must have the basis vectors as columns, in the chosen order.

sections.h3: The matrix of T in chosen bases

blocks.text: Take T: V → W linear, B = (b<sub>1</sub>, ..., b<sub>n</sub>) a basis of V, and C = (c<sub>1</sub>, ..., c<sub>m</sub>) a basis of W. The matrix [T]<sub>C←B</sub> has size m × n. Its j-th column is [T(b<sub>j</sub>)]<sub>C</sub>, the coordinate vector of the output in basis C. To build it: apply T to each domain basis vector, write the result in the codomain basis, and place the column in order.

blocks.where: [T]<sub>C←B</sub> is the matrix of T from basis B to basis C; [v]<sub>B</sub> is the coordinate column of v in B; [T(v)]<sub>C</sub> is the coordinate column of the output in C.

blocks.text: Let A be the standard matrix of T when V = R<sup>n</sup> and W = R<sup>m</sup> with standard bases. Let B and C also name the matrices whose columns are those basis vectors. Then [T]<sub>C←B</sub> = C<sup>−1</sup>A B. If C is standard, C = I, so [T]<sub>E←B</sub> = A B. The order C<sup>−1</sup>A B matters. The matrix B acts first, changing B-coordinates to standard coordinates. Then A applies T. Then C<sup>−1</sup> changes standard coordinates to C-coordinates.

When domain and codomain use the same basis B, write [T]<sub>B</sub> for [T]<sub>B←B</sub>. With A the standard matrix and P the matrix whose columns are B, [T]<sub>B</sub> = P<sup>−1</sup>A P. This operation is conjugation. Two matrices related this way represent the same linear map in two bases. They are called similar; Unit 4 studies similarity and diagonalization in detail.

Use it when the standard matrix is messy. A basis of eigenvectors, for example, can make the matrix diagonal, but finding eigenvectors belongs to Unit 4. For now, use conjugation only to translate between bases. Keep the two P matrices on the correct sides. A quick check: the size of P<sup>−1</sup>A P must equal the size of A, and its columns must be the coordinate vectors of T(b<sub>j</sub>) in B.

spec.title: Columns of [T]_B for B = {(1,1), (1,2)}
spec.aria: A two-row array shows the two columns of the matrix of T in basis B: the first column is (8, −5) and the second is (13, −9).

examples.question: Let T: R² → R² be T(x, y) = (2x + y, x − 3y), and let B = {(1, 1), (1, 2)}. Find [T]<sub>B</sub> by building its columns, then check using P<sup>−1</sup>A P.
steps: First column: T(1,1) = (2·1 + 1, 1 − 3·1) = (3,−2). Solve (3,−2) = c<sub>1</sub>(1,1) + c<sub>2</sub>(1,2). Equations c<sub>1</sub> + c<sub>2</sub> = 3, c<sub>1</sub> + 2c<sub>2</sub> = −2 give c<sub>2</sub> = −5, c<sub>1</sub> = 8. So [T(1,1)]<sub>B</sub> = (8,−5)<sup>T</sup>.

Second column: T(1,2) = (2·1 + 2, 1 − 3·2) = (4,−5). Solve c<sub>1</sub> + c<sub>2</sub> = 4, c<sub>1</sub> + 2c<sub>2</sub> = −5. Subtract: c<sub>2</sub> = −9, c<sub>1</sub> = 13. So [T(1,2)]<sub>B</sub> = (13,−9)<sup>T</sup>.
examples.check:
from fractions import Fraction
A = [[2, 1], [1, -3]]
P = [[1, 1], [1, 2]]
det = P[0][0]*P[1][1] - P[0][1]*P[1][0]
Pinv = [[Fraction(P[1][1], det), Fraction(-P[0][1], det)],
        [Fraction(-P[1][0], det), Fraction(P[0][0], det)]]
def mul(X, Y):
    return [[sum(X[i][k]*Y[k][j] for k in range(len(Y))) for j in range(len(Y[0]))] for i in range(len(X))]
M = mul(Pinv, mul(A, P))
for row in M:
    for x in row:
        print(int(x))

traps: Basis order matters: swapping b<sub>1</sub> and b<sub>2</sub> swaps the columns of P and permutes the rows of [T]<sub>B</sub>.
For different domain and codomain bases use [T]<sub>C←B</sub> = C<sup>−1</sup>A B, not B<sup>−1</sup>A C.
Do not put T(b<sub>j</sub>) in standard coordinates into the B-matrix without converting; the j-th column is [T(b<sub>j</sub>)]<sub>C</sub>, a coordinate vector.
A common slip is to write P<sup>−1</sup>A P with P columns in one order and the coordinate columns in another order.

quiz.q: Define the coordinate vector [v]<sub>B</sub> of v in an ordered basis B.
quiz.a: If B = (b<sub>1</sub>, ..., b<sub>n</sub>) and v = c<sub>1</sub>b<sub>1</sub> + ... + c<sub>n</sub>b<sub>n</sub>, then [v]<sub>B</sub> = (c<sub>1</sub>, ..., c<sub>n</sub>)<sup>T</sup>.

Write v as a combination of B vectors. Linearity sends it to the same combination of T(b<sub>j</sub>). Taking C-coordinates is linear, and the columns of [T]<sub>C←B</sub> are the C-coordinates of T(b<sub>j</sub>). So matrix multiplication reproduces the result.

quiz.q: For T(x,y) = (x + 2y, 3x − y) and B = {(1,1), (1,0)}, find [T]<sub>B</sub>.

quiz.a: Solve a(1,0) + b(1,1) = (a+b, b) = (4,3). Then b = 3 and a = 1, so [v]<sub>B</sub> = (1,3)<sup>T</sup>.

quiz.q: If [T]<sub>C←B</sub> is the zero matrix, what is T?
quiz.a: Every T(b<sub>j</sub>) has zero C-coordinate, so T(b<sub>j</sub>) = 0. Since the b<sub>j</sub> span V, linearity gives T(v) = 0 for every v. So T is the zero map.

quiz.q: V has dimension 2 and W has dimension 3. What size is [T]<sub>C←B</sub>?
quiz.a: The matrix has 3 rows and 2 columns, so size 3 × 2: one column for each domain basis vector and one row for each codomain coordinate.

quiz.q: What does [T]<sub>B</sub> = P<sup>−1</sup>A P mean in words?
quiz.a: It is the same linear map T written in basis B instead of the standard basis. P changes B-coordinates to standard coordinates, A applies T, and P<sup>−1</sup> changes back to B-coordinates.

beyond: Not for the exam. Graphics engines store a rotation as a matrix in the camera basis, then change basis for world coordinates. Robotics uses the same conjugation idea for joint frames. Numerical software often chooses a basis that reduces fill-in or improves conditioning. Search for change of basis matrix, matrix representation of a linear map, and similarity transformation.
